{{Short description|Inequality in mathematics}}
'''Hardy's inequality''' is an [[inequality (mathematics)|inequality]] in [[mathematics]], named after [[G. H. Hardy]]. 

Its '''discrete version''' states that if <math>a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots </math> is a [[sequence]] of [[non-negative]] [[real number]]s, then for every real number ''p'' > 1 one has

:<math>\sum_{n=1}^\infty \left (\frac{a_1+a_2+\cdots +a_n}{n}\right )^p\leq\left (\frac{p}{p-1}\right )^p\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n^p.</math>

If the right-hand side is finite, equality holds [[if and only if]] <math>a_n = 0</math> for all ''n''.

An '''[[integral]] version''' of Hardy's inequality states the following: if ''f'' is a [[measurable function]] with non-negative values, then

:<math>\int_0^\infty \left (\frac{1}{x}\int_0^x f(t)\, dt\right)^p\, dx\le\left (\frac{p}{p-1}\right )^p\int_0^\infty f(x)^p\, dx.</math>

If the right-hand side is finite, equality holds [[if and only if]] ''f''(''x'') = 0 [[almost everywhere]].

Hardy's inequality was first published and proved (at least the discrete version with a worse constant) in 1920 in a note by Hardy.<ref name=Hardy1920>{{Cite journal | last1 = Hardy | first1 = G. H. | title = Note on a theorem of Hilbert | doi = 10.1007/BF01199965 | journal = Mathematische Zeitschrift | volume = 6 | issue = 3–4 | pages = 314–317 | year = 1920 | s2cid = 122571449 | url = https://zenodo.org/record/2411518 }}</ref> The original formulation was in an integral form slightly different from the above.

== Statements ==

=== General discrete Hardy inequality === 

The general weighted one dimensional version reads as follows:<ref name="Hardy_Littlewood_Polya">{{cite book |last1=Hardy |first1=G. H. |last2=Littlewood |first2=J.E. |last3=Pólya |first3=G. |title=Inequalities |date=1952 |location=Cambridge, UK |edition=Second}}</ref>{{rp|§332}}
if <math>a_n \ge 0</math>, <math>\lambda_n>0</math> and <math>p > 1</math>,
:<math>
\sum_{n = 1}^\infty \lambda_n 
\Bigl(
\frac{\lambda_1 a_1 + \dotsb + \lambda_n a_n}{\lambda_1 + \dotsb + \lambda_n}
\Bigr)^p
\le \Bigl(\frac{p}{p - 1} \Bigr)^p \sum_{n = 1}^\infty \lambda_n a_n^p.
</math>

=== General one-dimensional integral Hardy inequality === 

The general weighted one dimensional version reads as follows:<ref name="Hardy_Littlewood_Polya" />{{rp|§330}}
* If <math>\alpha + \tfrac{1}{p} < 1</math>, then 
:<math>\int_0^\infty \biggl(y^{\alpha - 1} \int_0^y x^{-\alpha} f(x)\,dx \biggr)^p \,dy \le 
\frac{1}{\bigl(1 - \alpha - \frac{1}{p}\bigr)^p} \int_0^\infty f(x)^p\, dx
</math> 
* If <math>\alpha + \tfrac{1}{p} > 1</math>, then 
:<math>\int_0^\infty \biggl(y^{\alpha - 1} \int_y^\infty x^{-\alpha} f(x)\,dx \biggr)^p\,dy \le 
\frac{1}{\bigl(\alpha + \frac{1}{p} - 1\bigr)^p} \int_0^\infty f(x)^p\, dx.
</math>
The more general case is weighted integral Hardy inequality

=== Weighted one-dimensional integral Hardy inequality === 
The statement is following: if <math> 1 < p \leq q < \infty </math> inequality 
:<math> \left( \int_{a}^{b}{\left( \int_a^x{f(t)}dt \right)^q u(x)}dx \right)^{1/q} \leq C \left( \int_{a}^{b} {f^p(x) v(x)} dx \right)^{1/p}
</math>
holds for <math> -\infty \leq a < b \leq \infty </math> with <math>u, v</math> measurable, positive on <math>(a, b)</math> and also <math>f(x) \geq 0</math> any measurable on <math>(a, b)</math>, if and only if
:<math> A = \sup_{x \in (a, b)}{\left( \int_{x}^{b} u(t)dt \right)^{1/q} \left( \int_{a}^{x} v^{1-p'}(t) dt \right)^{1/p'}} < \infty 
</math>
And if <math> 1 < q < p < \infty </math> inequality also holds if and only if
::<math> A = \left( \int_{a}^{b}{{\left( \int_{x}^{b} u(t)dt \right)^{r/q} \left( \int_{a}^{x} v^{1-p'}(t) dt \right)^{r/q'}}v^{1-p'}(x) dx} \right)^{1/r} < \infty 
</math>
where <math> \frac{1}{r} = \frac{1}{q} - \frac{1}{p}, \frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{p'} = 1 </math> and <math> \frac{1}{q} + \frac{1}{q'} = 1 </math>

===Multidimensional Hardy inequalities with gradient===

====Multidimensional Hardy inequality around a point====
In the multidimensional case, Hardy's inequality can be extended to <math>L^{p}</math>-spaces, taking the form <ref>{{cite book |last1=Ruzhansky |first1=Michael |last2=Suragan |first2=Durvudkhan |title=Hardy Inequalities on Homogeneous Groups: 100 Years of Hardy Inequalities |date=2019 |publisher=Birkhäuser Basel |isbn=978-3-030-02894-7 |url=https://www.springer.com/gp/book/9783030028947 |language=en}}</ref>

:<math>\left\|\frac{f}{|\cdot|}\right\|_{L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}\le \frac{p}{n-p}\|\nabla f\|_{L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}, 2\le n, 1\le p<n,</math>
where <math>f\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n})</math>, and where the constant <math>\frac{p}{n-p}</math> is known to be sharp; by density it extends then to the [[Sobolev space]] <math>W^{1, p} (\mathbb{R}^n)</math>.

Similarly, if <math>p > n \ge 2</math>, then one has for every <math>f\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n})</math>
:<math>
 \Big(1 - \frac{n}{p}\Big)^p  \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \frac{\vert f(x) - f (0)\vert^p}{|x|^p} dx 
\le \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \vert \nabla f\vert^p.
</math>

====Multidimensional Hardy inequality near the boundary====

If <math>\Omega \subsetneq \mathbb{R}^n</math> is an nonempty [[wikt:Convex|convex]] [[open set]], then for <math>1<p<\infty</math> and every <math>f \in W_0^{1, p} (\Omega)</math>,
:<math>
 \Big(1 - \frac{1}{p}\Big)^p\int_{\Omega} \frac{\vert f (x)\vert^p}{\operatorname{dist} (x, \partial \Omega)^p}\,dx
\le \int_{\Omega}\vert \nabla f \vert^p,
</math>
and the constant cannot be improved.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Marcus |first1=Moshe |last2=Mizel |first2=Victor J. |last3=Pinchover |first3=Yehuda |title=On the best constant for Hardy's inequality in $\mathbb {R}^n$ |journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society |date=1998 |volume=350 |issue=8 |pages=3237–3255 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9947-98-02122-9|doi-access=free }}</ref>

===Fractional Hardy inequality===

If <math>1 \le p < \infty</math> and <math>0 < \lambda < \infty</math>, <math>\lambda \ne 1</math>, there exists a constant <math>C</math> such that for every <math>f : (0, \infty) \to \mathbb{R}</math> satisfying <math>\int_0^\infty \vert f (x)\vert^p/x^{\lambda} \,dx < \infty</math>, one has<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mironescu |first1=Petru |title=The role of the Hardy type inequalities in the theory of function spaces |journal=Revue roumaine de mathématiques pures et appliquées |date=2018 |volume=63 |issue=4 |pages=447–525 |url=http://imar.ro/journals/Revue_Mathematique/pdfs/2018/4/7.pdf}}</ref>{{rp|Lemma 2}}
:<math>
\int_0^\infty \frac{\vert f (x)\vert^p}{x^{\lambda}} \,dx 
\le C \int_0^\infty \int_0^\infty \frac{\vert f (x) - f (y)\vert^p}{\vert x - y\vert^{1+\lambda}} \,dx \, dy.
</math>

==Proof of the inequality==
=== Integral version (integration by parts and Hölder) ===
Hardy’s original proof<ref name=Hardy1920 /><ref name="Hardy_Littlewood_Polya" />{{rp|§327 (ii)}} begins with an [[integration by parts]] to get
:<math>
\begin{align}
\int_0^\infty \left(\frac{1}{x} \int_0^x f(t)\, dt \right)^p dx
&= \int_0^\infty \left(\int_0^x f(t)\, dt \right)^p \frac{1}{x^p} dx
\\[0.2em]
&= \frac{p}{p - 1} \int_0^\infty
\left(\int_0^x f(t)\, dt \right)^{p - 1} \frac{f (x)}{x^{p - 1}} dx \\[0.2em]
&= \frac{p}{p - 1} \int_0^\infty
\left(\frac{1}{x}\int_0^x f(t)\, dt \right)^{p - 1} f (x) dx
\end{align}
</math>
Then, by [[Hölder's inequality]],
:<math>
\int_0^\infty \left(\frac{1}{x} \int_0^x f(t)\, dt \right)^p dx
\le \frac{p}{p - 1} \left( \int_0^\infty \left(\frac{1}{x} \int_0^x f(t)\, dt \right)^p dx \right)^{1 - \frac{1}{p}}
 \left( \int_0^\infty f (x)^p \, dx \right)^\frac{1}{p},
</math>
and the conclusion follows.

=== Integral version (scaling and Minkowski) ===
A [[Integration by substitution|change of variables]] gives 
:<math>\left(\int_0^\infty\left(\frac{1}{x}\int_0^x f(t)\,dt\right)^p\ dx\right)^{1/p}=\left(\int_0^\infty\left(\int_0^1 f(sx)\,ds\right)^p\,dx\right)^{1/p},</math>
which is less or equal than <math>\int_0^1\left(\int_0^\infty f(sx)^p\,dx\right)^{1/p}\,ds</math> by [[Minkowski inequality#Minkowski's integral inequality|Minkowski's integral inequality]]. 
Finally, by another change of variables, the last expression equals 
:<math>\int_0^1\left(\int_0^\infty f(x)^p\,dx\right)^{1/p}s^{-1/p}\,ds=\frac{p}{p-1}\left(\int_0^\infty f(x)^p\,dx\right)^{1/p}.</math>

=== Discrete version: from the continuous version ===
Assuming the right-hand side to be finite, we must have <math>a_n\to 0</math> as <math>n\to\infty</math>. Hence, for any positive integer {{math|''j''}}, there are only finitely many terms bigger than <math>2^{-j}</math>. 
This allows us to construct a decreasing sequence <math>b_1\ge b_2\ge\dotsb</math> containing the same positive terms as the original sequence (but possibly no zero terms). Since <math>a_1+a_2+\dotsb +a_n\le b_1+b_2+\dotsb +b_n</math> for every {{math|''n''}}, it suffices to show the inequality for the new sequence. This follows directly from the integral form, defining <math>f(x)=b_n</math> if <math>n-1<x<n</math> and <math>f(x)=0</math> otherwise. Indeed, one has 
:<math>\int_0^\infty f(x)^p\,dx=\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n^p</math> 
and, for <math>n-1<x<n</math>, there holds 
:<math>\frac{1}{x}\int_0^x f(t)\,dt=\frac{b_1+\dots+b_{n-1}+(x-n+1)b_n}{x} \ge \frac{b_1+\dots+b_n}{n}</math>
(the last inequality is equivalent to <math>(n-x)(b_1+\dots+b_{n-1})\ge (n-1)(n-x)b_n</math>, which is true as the new sequence is decreasing) and thus 
:<math>\sum_{n=1}^\infty\left(\frac{b_1+\dots+b_n}{n}\right)^p\le\int_0^\infty\left(\frac{1}{x}\int_0^x f(t)\,dt\right)^p\,dx</math>.

=== Discrete version: Direct proof===

Let <math>p > 1</math> and let <math>b_1 , \dots , b_n</math> be positive real numbers. Set <math>S_k = \sum_{i=1}^k b_i</math>. 
First we prove the inequality 
{{NumBlk|:|<math>\sum_{n=1}^N \frac{S_n^p}{n^p} \leq \frac{p}{p-1} \sum_{n=1}^N \frac{b_n S_n^{p-1}}{n^{p-1}},</math>|{{EquationRef|&ast;}}}}

Let <math>T_n = \frac{S_n}{n}</math> and let <math>\Delta_n</math> be the difference between the <math>n</math>-th terms in the right-hand side and left-hand side of {{EquationNote|*}}, that is, <math>\Delta_n := T_n^p - \frac{p}{p-1} b_n T_n^{p-1}</math>. We have: 

:<math>\Delta_n = T_n^p - \frac{p}{p-1} b_n T_n^{p-1} = T_n^p - \frac{p}{p-1} (n T_n - (n-1) T_{n-1}) T_n^{p-1}</math>

or

:<math>\Delta_n = T_n^p \left( 1 - \frac{np}{p-1} \right) + \frac{p (n-1)}{p-1} T_{n-1} T_n^p  .</math>

According to [[Young's inequality for products|Young's inequality]] we have:

:<math>T_{n-1} T_n^{p-1} \leq \frac{T_{n-1}^p}{p} + (p-1) \frac{T_n^p}{p}  ,</math>

from which it follows that:

:<math>\Delta_n \leq \frac{n-1}{p-1} T_{n-1}^p - \frac{n}{p-1} T_n^p  .</math>

By telescoping we have:

:<math>
\begin{align}
\sum_{n=1}^N \Delta_n &\leq 0 - \frac{1}{p-1} T_1^p + \frac{1}{p-1} T_1^p
- \frac{2}{p-1} T_2^p + \frac{2}{p-1} T_2^p - \\
& \qquad - \frac{3}{p-1} T_3^p + \dotsb 
+ \frac{N-1}{p-1} T_{N-1}^p - \frac{N}{p-1} T_N^p \\
& \qquad = - \frac{N}{p-1} T_N^p < 0
\end{align}
</math>

proving {{EquationNote|*}}. 
Applying [[Hölder's inequality]] to the right-hand side of {{EquationNote|*}} we have:

:<math>\sum_{n=1}^N \frac{S_n^p}{n^p} \leq \frac{p}{p-1} \sum_{n=1}^N \frac{b_n S_n^{p-1}}{n^{p-1}} \leq \frac{p}{p-1} \left( \sum_{n=1}^N b_n^p \right)^{1/p} \left( \sum_{n=1}^N \frac{S_n^p}{n^p} \right)^{(p-1)/p}</math>

from which we immediately obtain:

:<math>\sum_{n=1}^N \frac{S_n^p}{n^p} \leq \left( \frac{p}{p-1} \right)^p \sum_{n=1}^N b_n^p  .</math>

Letting <math>N \rightarrow \infty</math> we obtain Hardy's inequality.
